README.md.overview: The project's front door. It introduces TradingAgents as a multi-agent LLM framework modeled on a trading firm (analysts, bull/bear researchers, trader, risk team, portfolio manager), then covers installation, Docker, API keys, the CLI, Python package usage, persistence and evaluation. Tour step 1 uses it to establish the cast of roles that later steps map to code.

sections.title: Header and Trading-R1 banner
sections.explanation: Logo, badges (arXiv paper, Discord, X) and a promotion of the sibling Trading-R1 project. Purely presentational HTML embedded in Markdown so it renders centered on GitHub.

sections.title: Release news
sections.explanation: A changelog-style news list wrapped in `<!-- news:start -->` / `<!-- news:end -->` markers, which suggests it is maintained or extracted by tooling. Older entries are folded into a `<details>` block. Skimming it is a quick way to learn which features are recent, such as per-tier providers, parallel analysts and checkpoint resume.

sections.title: Framework roles
sections.explanation: The conceptual core of the README: the Analyst Team (fundamentals, sentiment, news, technical), the bull/bear Researcher Team, the Trader, and the Risk Management team plus Portfolio Manager. It notes that the selected analysts run concurrently and the research debate starts once every report is in. Keep this role list in mind; each later tour step maps one of them to code.

sections.title: Installation, Docker and API keys
sections.explanation: Install steps (Python 3.11+, `pip install .`), a Docker Compose path with an optional Ollama profile, and the full list of provider API-key environment variables. It also explains the special providers: ChatGPT plan sign-in, AWS Bedrock via the `bedrock` extra, Ollama, and generic `openai_compatible` endpoints. These map directly onto `.env.example` and the provider registry in `openai_client.py`.

sections.title: CLI usage and markets
sections.explanation: How to launch the interactive `tradingagents` command or run it headless with flags plus `TRADINGAGENTS_*` variables, and which exchange-suffixed tickers are supported. The suffixes here (`.HK`, `.T`, `.NS`, ...) correspond to the `benchmark_map` in `default_config.py`.

sections.title: Python package usage
sections.explanation: Shows the minimal `TradingAgentsGraph(...).propagate(ticker, date)` call that `main.py` reproduces, how to tweak `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, and how to put the deep (manager) and quick (analyst) tiers on different providers. Also documents point-in-time SEC EDGAR fundamentals and passing a `PortfolioContext` so agents reason about current holdings.

sections.title: Persistence and evaluation
sections.explanation: Describes the always-on memory log of past decisions, opt-in per-ticker SQLite checkpoint resume, `run_backtest` over a ticker/date grid, and an honest reproducibility section explaining why LLM-driven runs vary and how `temperature` helps only for non-reasoning models.

sections.title: Contributing and citation
sections.explanation: Contribution pointer to `CHANGELOG.md` and the BibTeX entry for the arXiv paper (2412.20138).

main.py.overview: The smallest working use of the library: copy the default config, build a TradingAgentsGraph in debug mode, and propagate one decision for NVDA on a fixed date. Tour step 2 presents it as the seed that every richer entry point, including the CLI, elaborates on.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in the two public building blocks: `DEFAULT_CONFIG` (built at import time from defaults plus environment overrides) and the `TradingAgentsGraph` orchestrator.

sections.title: Config copy
sections.explanation: The comment is the key lesson: because `DEFAULT_CONFIG` already folds in `TRADINGAGENTS_*` variables, switching models or endpoints needs only a `.env` change. `.copy()` is a shallow copy, so the script can override top-level keys without mutating the module-level default; nested dicts like `data_vendors` would still be shared.

sections.title: Build graph and propagate
sections.explanation: `debug=True` makes the graph trace its progress. `propagate` returns a pair (final state, decision); the script discards the state with `_` and prints just the decision. The README shows the same call keeping the state to pass to `save_reports`.

pyproject.toml.overview: Declares the `tradingagents` distribution: setuptools build backend, runtime dependencies (LangChain provider packages, LangGraph with SQLite checkpointing, yfinance, rich, typer, questionary), optional extras, the console script, and tool settings for pytest and ruff. Tour step 2 uses it to show how the package and its `tradingagents` command are defined.

sections.title: Build system and metadata
sections.explanation: Uses setuptools via PEP 517. The version is `dynamic`, resolved later from `tradingagents.__version__`, so there is a single place to bump it. Python 3.11+ is required, matching the `X | None` syntax and other modern features used throughout.

sections.title: Runtime dependencies
sections.explanation: One LangChain integration per native provider (Anthropic, Google GenAI, OpenAI), LangGraph plus `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite` for resumable runs, `python-dotenv` for `.env` loading, data libraries (pandas, yfinance, stockstats) and CLI libraries (rich, typer, questionary). Note there is no separate package per OpenAI-compatible provider: they all go through `langchain-openai`.

sections.title: Optional extras
sections.explanation: `dev` adds ruff and pytest; `bedrock` adds `langchain-aws` only for users who need Amazon Bedrock, keeping the core install lean. Install with `pip install "tradingagents[bedrock]"`.

sections.title: Console script and packaging
sections.explanation: `[project.scripts]` maps the shell command `tradingagents` to the Typer app object `cli.main:app`. Package discovery includes both `tradingagents*` and `cli*`, and package-data ships the CLI's static files and the SVG assets.

sections.title: Pytest configuration
sections.explanation: Defines `unit`, `integration` and `smoke` markers with `--strict-markers`, and excludes integration tests by default (`-m "not integration"`) so a plain `pytest` never hits external services.

sections.title: Ruff lint configuration
sections.explanation: Line length 100 targeting py311, a curated rule set (pyflakes, pycodestyle, isort, bugbear, pyupgrade, comprehensions, simplify) with E501 ignored. `F401` is ignored in `__init__.py` for intentional re-exports, and `combine-as-imports` keeps aliased vendor imports in one block.

.env.example.overview: A template for the `.env` file that `tradingagents/__init__.py` loads at import. It lists the API key for every supported LLM provider, optional data-service keys, and commented-out `TRADINGAGENTS_*` overrides that map one-to-one onto `_ENV_OVERRIDES` in `default_config.py`. Tour step 3 uses it to show where secrets and settings enter the system.

sections.title: LLM provider keys
sections.explanation: One key per provider; you only need to fill the one you use. Dual-region providers (DashScope/Qwen, Zhipu/GLM, MiniMax) have separate `_CN_` keys because international and China accounts cannot share credentials, matching the separate registry rows in `openai_client.py`.

sections.title: Data-service keys
sections.explanation: Optional keys for SEC EDGAR (a contact User-Agent rather than a secret), FRED macro data, and TypeSafe Jev social-post screening. All are commented out, so the defaults work without them.

sections.title: Alternative LLM backends
sections.explanation: Settings for providers that don't use a plain API key: a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint, AWS Bedrock (bearer token or credential chain plus region), ChatGPT plan sign-in, and a remote Ollama base URL (`OLLAMA_BASE_URL`, which the Ollama `ProviderSpec` reads via `base_url_env`).

sections.title: TRADINGAGENTS_* config overrides
sections.explanation: Commented examples of every environment override: provider and models, per-tier provider/backend URLs, output language, debate and tool round limits, checkpointing, paths, benchmark, temperature, retries, token cap and per-provider reasoning effort. Each name corresponds to a row in `_ENV_OVERRIDES` (or a path variable read directly in `build_default_config`), and values are plain strings coerced by type.

tradingagents/__init__.py.overview: The package root. It defines `__version__` (read by setuptools for the distribution version) and loads `.env` files as a side effect of import, so every entry point sees API keys and `TRADINGAGENTS_*` overrides before `default_config` builds `DEFAULT_CONFIG`. Tour step 3 highlights this import-time loading.

sections.title: Version
sections.explanation: `__version__` is the single source of the package version; `pyproject.toml` reads it via `[tool.setuptools.dynamic]`.

sections.title: Import-time .env loading
sections.explanation: `find_dotenv(usecwd=True)` searches from the current working directory, so an installed console script finds the project's `.env` instead of looking next to site-packages. `load_dotenv` never overrides variables already exported in the shell. A second optional `.env.enterprise` file (used for Azure OpenAI credentials per the README) is loaded the same way. Because this runs on `import tradingagents`, it happens before any submodule such as `default_config` reads the environment.

tradingagents/dataflows/config.py.overview: Holds the configuration that data tools read. It keeps a process-wide config (deep-copied from DEFAULT_CONFIG) plus a per-run override stored in a `ContextVar`, so several TradingAgentsGraph instances in one process each see their own vendor settings. Tour step 3 introduces it as the mechanism that keeps concurrent runs isolated.

sections.title: Module state
sections.explanation: Two layers: `_config`, a mutable process-wide dict, and `_run_config`, a `ContextVar` defaulting to `None`. The comment notes that LangGraph carries the context into tool calls, which is what makes the per-run value visible inside data tools without passing it explicitly.

sections.title: Initialize and merge
sections.explanation: `initialize_config` lazily deep-copies the defaults once. `_merge` does a one-level-deep merge: nested dicts are updated key by key, scalars are replaced. It deep-copies the incoming config first so callers can't later mutate shared state through it.

sections.title: set_config
sections.explanation: Applies a partial update to the process-wide config. The docstring example shows why the shallow merge matters: setting only `core_stock_apis` inside `data_vendors` keeps the other vendor categories from the default.

sections.title: Per-run scoping
sections.explanation: `run_config` is a context manager that sets the ContextVar to defaults-plus-overrides and restores it with the token in `finally`. `run_config_context` instead returns a copied `Context` with the value set; this suits a streamed run that yields between steps, where a `with` block would otherwise stay open in the caller's context. Both build from DEFAULT_CONFIG, not from the process-wide `_config`.

sections.title: get_config
sections.explanation: Reads the run-scoped config if one is active, else the process-wide one, always returning a deep copy so readers can't mutate shared state. The final `initialize_config()` call ensures `_config` is populated at import.

tradingagents/default_config.py.overview: The most depended-on module in the project. It defines every built-in default (paths, LLM provider and models, per-tier overrides, sampling and retry settings, debate limits, news parameters, data vendors, benchmarks) and folds in `TRADINGAGENTS_*` environment variables with coercion driven by the type of each default. Tour step 3 centers on it.

sections.title: Env-var override table
sections.explanation: `_ENV_OVERRIDES` is the single source of truth mapping environment variable names to config keys. Exposing a new key to the environment means adding one row here, with no entry-point changes. Path variables are not in this table; they are read directly in `build_default_config`.

sections.title: Type-driven coercion
sections.explanation: `_coerce` converts the env string to the type of the existing default: accepted boolean spellings, `int`, or `float`. The `bool` check comes first because `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python. Invalid values raise `ValueError` instead of silently falling back, so a typo like `treu` fails loudly at startup. One consequence: keys whose default is `None` (for example `temperature`, `max_tokens`) stay strings, and are converted later in `factory.build_llm_kwargs`.

sections.title: Applying overrides
sections.explanation: Iterates the table, skips unset or empty variables, coerces, and rewraps errors so the message names the offending variable.

sections.title: Paths and LLM settings
sections.explanation: `build_default_config` returns a fresh dict each call. Paths default under `~/.tradingagents`. LLM defaults are the OpenAI provider with separate deep and quick models; `backend_url` defaults to `None` so each provider uses its own endpoint (the comment explains a past bug where OpenAI's URL leaked to Gemini). Per-tier `*_think_provider` and `*_think_backend_url` let the managers and analysts run on different providers. `None` for temperature, retries and max_tokens means 'leave the provider's own default'.

sections.title: Tool rounds and news parameters
sections.explanation: `max_tool_rounds` bounds how many tool-call rounds an analyst may take before it is asked for its report. News limits and `global_news_queries` tune how much macro context reaches the prompts, trading coverage against token usage.

sections.title: Data vendors
sections.explanation: `data_vendors` sets a vendor chain per category, and the comment stresses that requests are never silently routed to unchosen vendors; a comma list like `sec_edgar,yfinance` gives ordered fallback. `tool_vendors` overrides individual tools. This nested dict is what `dataflows/config.py`'s one-level merge is designed for.

sections.title: Benchmarks and DEFAULT_CONFIG
sections.explanation: `holding_period_days` sets how many trading days after the first post-decision close are used to score an outcome. `benchmark_map` picks a regional index from the ticker's exchange suffix, with `""` mapping US tickers to SPY; `benchmark_ticker` overrides it globally. `DEFAULT_CONFIG` is evaluated once at import; call `build_default_config()` again to pick up later environment changes.

tradingagents/llm_clients/anthropic_clie.overview: The native Anthropic (Claude) client. It wraps `ChatAnthropic` so responses come back as plain strings, forwards a whitelist of user kwargs, and passes the extended-thinking `effort` parameter only to models known to accept it. Tour step 4 presents it as one of the concrete BaseLLMClient implementations the factory can build.

sections.title: Imports and passthrough kwargs
sections.explanation: `_PASSTHROUGH_KWARGS` is an explicit whitelist of settings forwarded to `ChatAnthropic`, so unrelated config keys never reach the SDK. `effort` is included but gated below.

sections.title: Effort-capable model rules
sections.explanation: The comment documents the API behavior: Opus 4.5+, Sonnet 4.6+ and the Claude 5 family accept `effort`, while Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku return HTTP 400. `_EFFORT_MODEL` parses family, major and optional minor version, and ignores a trailing 8-digit snapshot date so it isn't mistaken for a minor version. `_EFFORT_EXACT` covers non-standard names.

sections.title: _supports_effort
sections.explanation: Checks exact names first, then compares the parsed `(major, minor)` tuple against the per-family minimum. Tuple comparison makes this forward-compatible: any future version above the minimum passes without code changes. Unrecognized names return `False`, so effort is dropped rather than risking a 400.

sections.title: NormalizedChatAnthropic
sections.explanation: A thin subclass overriding `invoke` to run `normalize_content`, because Claude with extended thinking or tool use returns a list of typed content blocks and downstream agents expect a string.

sections.title: AnthropicClient
sections.explanation: `get_llm` warns on unknown models, adds `base_url` only if set, copies whitelisted kwargs while skipping `effort` for unsupported models, and returns the normalized chat model. `validate_model` delegates to the shared validators module.

tradingagents/llm_clients/base_client.py.overview: Defines the abstract interface every LLM client implements and a shared helper that flattens provider-specific content blocks into a plain string. Tour step 4 uses it as the contract that lets agents depend on one interface while the factory picks the concrete provider.

sections.title: normalize_content
sections.explanation: Some APIs (OpenAI Responses, Gemini 3, Claude with thinking) return `content` as a list of typed blocks. This helper keeps only `text` blocks and bare strings, drops reasoning/metadata blocks, and joins them with newlines. It mutates and returns the response so callers can wrap `super().invoke(...)` in one expression, as the provider subclasses do.

sections.title: BaseLLMClient core
sections.explanation: Stores model, base URL and arbitrary kwargs. `get_provider_name` prefers an explicit `provider` attribute (set by `OpenAIClient`, which serves many providers) and otherwise derives a name from the class, e.g. `AnthropicClient` becomes `anthropic`. `warn_if_unknown_model` emits a `RuntimeWarning` but continues, so new models work before the known-model list is updated.

sections.title: Abstract methods
sections.explanation: `get_llm` returns the configured LangChain chat model and `validate_model` reports whether the model is known. Using `abc.abstractmethod` means a subclass that forgets either cannot be instantiated.

tradingagents/llm_clients/capabilities.p.overview: A declarative table of what each OpenAI-compatible model accepts: tool_choice, JSON mode, JSON schema, the preferred structured-output method, and provider quirks like DeepSeek's reasoning-content round trip and MiniMax's reasoning split. Clients call `get_capabilities` instead of hardcoding model-name branches. Tour step 4 describes it as the record of per-model parameter support.

sections.title: Module docstring and method type
sections.explanation: Explains the design: adding a model or quirk means editing this table, not client code. `StructuredMethod` is a `Literal` type enumerating the structured-output strategies, with `none` meaning callers fall back to free text.

sections.title: ModelCapabilities dataclass
sections.explanation: A frozen dataclass so profiles are immutable and can be shared safely. The two quirk flags default to `False`; the comments record the concrete failures they prevent (DeepSeek 400s without echoed reasoning_content; MiniMax non-reasoning models reject `reasoning_split`).

sections.title: Capability profiles
sections.explanation: Reusable profiles: DeepSeek thinking models reject `tool_choice` and need the reasoning round trip; DeepSeek chat is ordinary; MiniMax M2.x only accept the string enum for tool_choice, so it is suppressed and `reasoning_split` is required; `_DEFAULT` supports everything. All use `function_calling`, so the schema is still bound as a tool even when `tool_choice` is withheld.

sections.title: Lookup tables
sections.explanation: `_BY_ID` maps exact model IDs to profiles; `_BY_PATTERN` uses anchored regexes so future `deepseek-v5-*` or `MiniMax-M3*` models inherit the quirks automatically.

sections.title: get_capabilities
sections.explanation: Resolution order is exact ID, then pattern, then default. It first strips OpenRouter's official `deepseek/` namespace so routed DeepSeek models get native quirks, but deliberately leaves other publishers' finetunes on the default because their behavior is unknown.

tradingagents/llm_clients/factory.py.overview: The Factory that turns config into an LLM client. `create_llm_client` lazily imports the right provider module, `build_llm_kwargs` translates TradingAgents config into provider-specific kwargs, and `create_tier_client` builds the quick or deep tier client, each possibly on its own provider and endpoint. Tour step 4 starts here.

sections.title: create_llm_client
sections.explanation: Native APIs (Anthropic, Google, Azure, Bedrock) are matched first, each importing its module only inside its branch. This lazy import keeps test collection and plain imports from loading heavy SDKs or failing on missing keys, and means Bedrock's optional dependency is only needed when used. Everything else goes through the OpenAI-compatible registry; an unknown name raises `ValueError`.

sections.title: Retry and token validators
sections.explanation: Env vars arrive as strings and default `None` keys are not coerced by `default_config`, so these accept ints or numeric strings. Booleans are rejected explicitly (since `True` would otherwise become `1`), as are negatives for retries and non-positive token caps, to fail at startup instead of silently misconfiguring.

sections.title: build_llm_kwargs
sections.explanation: Maps provider-specific reasoning knobs: Google's `thinking_level`, OpenAI/ChatGPT's `reasoning_effort`, Anthropic's `effort`. Then forwards cross-provider settings only when set, so each SDK otherwise keeps its own defaults. `temperature` is cast with `float()`, and the token cap is renamed to `max_output_tokens` for Google.

sections.title: Tier resolution
sections.explanation: `tier_provider` returns the tier's own provider or falls back to `llm_provider`. In `create_tier_client`, the shared `backend_url` applies only when the tier uses the main provider, because that URL belongs to `llm_provider`; a tier on another provider uses its own `*_think_backend_url` or the provider default. Kwargs are rebuilt with `llm_provider` swapped to the tier's provider so the right reasoning knob and token-cap name are used.

tradingagents/llm_clients/openai_client..overview: One client for the whole OpenAI-compatible family (OpenAI, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, MiniMax, OpenRouter, Mistral, Kimi, Groq, NVIDIA, Ollama, ChatGPT plan, and any custom endpoint). Provider differences are expressed as `ProviderSpec` rows plus small `ChatOpenAI` subclasses for wire-format quirks, and structured output consults `capabilities.py`. Tour step 4 describes this declarative registry.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Note the dependencies on `api_key_env` (the single source of API-key variable names, shared with the CLI), `capabilities`, and the shared validators.

sections.title: NormalizedChatOpenAI
sections.explanation: The base chat class. `invoke` flattens Responses-API content blocks to a string. `with_structured_output` looks up the model's capabilities, raises `NotImplementedError` when none exist (agent factories catch this and fall back to free text), and when the model rejects `tool_choice` it sets `tool_choice=None` while still binding the schema as a tool.

sections.title: Local server variant and input helper
sections.explanation: `LocalCompatibleChatOpenAI` always suppresses `tool_choice` for function calling, because local servers (LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp) vary in support regardless of model ID. `_input_to_messages` accepts both message lists and `ChatPromptValue` objects; the docstring warns that handling only lists would silently skip template-driven call sites.

sections.title: DeepSeek reasoning round trip
sections.explanation: Overrides two LangChain internals: `_create_chat_result` copies `reasoning_content` from the raw response into the message's `additional_kwargs`, and `_get_request_payload` re-attaches it to outgoing assistant messages. Without this, DeepSeek thinking models return HTTP 400 on the next turn.

sections.title: MiniMax and ChatGPT plan variants
sections.explanation: `MinimaxChatOpenAI` sets `reasoning_split=True` through `extra_body` (the OpenAI SDK rejects unknown top-level params), only for models whose capabilities require it. `ChatGPTPlanChatOpenAI` drops refused settings with a warning, forces streaming and `store=False`, clears org/project IDs so API-key settings never travel with the sign-in, and rewrites `system` roles to `developer`. `_chatgpt_credential` lazily imports the auth module.

sections.title: Passthrough and reasoning gate
sections.explanation: Whitelisted kwargs forwarded to the chat class. `_OPENAI_REASONING_MODEL` matches GPT-5 and later and the o-series, so `reasoning_effort` is dropped for non-reasoning models that would 400.

sections.title: ProviderSpec registry
sections.explanation: `ProviderSpec` is a frozen dataclass of per-provider fields: chat subclass, default and env-overridable base URL, key optionality and placeholder, required base URL, Responses API use, sign-in credential, and endpoint pinning. `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_PROVIDERS` is the single source of truth; dual-region providers get separate rows. `SIGNED_IN_PROVIDERS` is derived from the table rather than listed by hand.

sections.title: Endpoint helpers
sections.explanation: `check_endpoint` refuses to send a pinned provider's token (ChatGPT) to any other URL. `is_openai_compatible` is what the factory uses for routing. `_is_native_openai_base_url` keeps the Responses API off when the `openai` provider points at a proxy or local server, since only api.openai.com serves `/v1/responses`.

sections.title: OpenAIClient.get_llm
sections.explanation: Assembles the chat model from the spec. Base URL precedence is explicit client value, then the provider's env override, then the spec default. The API key comes from the sign-in credential, the provider's env var, or a placeholder for keyless servers; a missing required key raises an error naming the variable to set. Finally it forwards gated passthrough kwargs and instantiates the spec's chat class.

tradingagents/agents/rating.py.overview: Defines the shared five-tier rating vocabulary (Buy, Overweight, Hold, Underweight, Sell) and a deterministic parser that reads a rating out of free-text decisions. The Research Manager, Portfolio Manager and memory log all depend on it, so keeping it in one module prevents the scale from drifting between call sites. Its key design rule, highlighted in tour step 5, is that an unreadable decision becomes the non-tradeable `REVIEW` sentinel instead of silently defaulting to Hold.

sections.title: Module purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The module docstring explains which components share the scale and why `extract_rating` returns `None` on failure: a Hold recorded for an unreadable decision would be quoted back to later runs as a call that was never made (issue #1170). Only `re` and `unicodedata` are needed, so this module has no dependency on LangChain or the rest of the framework.

sections.title: Rating constants
sections.explanation: `RATINGS_5_TIER` is an ordered tuple from most bullish to most bearish, and `RATING_REVIEW` is the sentinel for a decision with no recognizable rating. The comment warns callers to check `is_review` before converting a signal into the `PortfolioRating` enum, because `REVIEW` is not a member of it. `_RATING_SET` is a lowercase set used for fast, case-insensitive membership checks.

sections.title: Rating regular expressions
sections.explanation: Three regexes encode what counts as a rating. `_RATING_LABEL_RE` finds any `rating: X` label, tolerating markdown bold and any Unicode dash or colon, and requires `rating` to start a word so `Operating margin: Sell-side` does not match. `_RATING_LINE_RE` matches the decision's own rating line, with an optional list marker and qualifiers such as 'final' or 'our', so `Consensus rating: Buy` is treated as someone else's rating. `_RATING_SCALE_RE` filters out lines where the model just echoed the scale legend.

sections.title: extract_rating heuristic
sections.explanation: The text is first NFKC-normalized so fullwidth punctuation (for example `Rating：Overweight`) parses like ASCII. A rating on the opening line (after headings) wins immediately unless it is a list item. Otherwise the function collects the decision's own rating lines, falling back to every label, and returns a value only when all candidates agree. Bare rating words in prose are deliberately ignored, since text such as 'not a Sell' would otherwise report a direction nobody chose.

sections.title: Convenience wrappers
sections.explanation: `parse_rating` always returns a string, defaulting to `REVIEW` and never to a tradeable rating, which suits the memory log's entry tag. `run_rating` prefers the Portfolio Manager's structured `final_rating` and falls back to parsing `final_trade_decision`, which covers states produced by older versions or restored from checkpoints. `is_review` is the guard callers use before mapping a signal to the enum.

tradingagents/agents/schemas.py.overview: Holds the Pydantic models that the decision-making agents (Research Manager, Trader, Portfolio Manager) and the Sentiment Analyst use for structured LLM output, plus render helpers that turn each parsed model back into markdown. Prose stays the main artifact; the schemas make section headers consistent across providers and let field descriptions act as output instructions. As tour step 5 explains, Pydantic validation and coercion handle the malformed values LLMs often produce.

sections.title: Design rationale and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring sets out the strategy: use each provider's native structured-output mode (json_schema, response_schema, tool use), let `Field` descriptions carry the instructions, and render the result back to the markdown the rest of the system already reads. `StrEnum` makes enum members behave as plain strings when they are serialized or compared.

sections.title: Optional float coercion
sections.explanation: `_coerce_optional_float` cleans LLM-written numeric fields before validation. Placeholder strings ('N/A', 'none') and percentages ('15%') become `None`, because a percentage cannot be turned into an absolute price level safely. Currency symbols and thousands separators are stripped. Anything that still is not a single number, such as a range or a hedge, is also dropped, so one bad field does not cause the whole decision to fail validation.

sections.title: Shared rating enums
sections.explanation: `PortfolioRating` mirrors the five-tier scale from rating.py for the Research Manager and Portfolio Manager. `TraderAction` is a coarser Buy/Hold/Sell scale, because the Trader only proposes a transaction direction and sizing nuance is left to the Portfolio Manager.

sections.title: ResearchPlan model and renderer
sections.explanation: The Research Manager's hand-off to the Trader has a recommendation, a rationale and strategic actions. The recommendation's description tells the model not to Hold just because arguments conflict, which counters LLMs' tendency to pick the middle. `render_research_plan` emits bold-labelled markdown sections for storage and for the trader's prompt.

sections.title: TraderProposal model and renderer
sections.explanation: The proposal holds an action, reasoning and optional entry price, stop loss and sizing. A `field_validator` with `mode='before'` sends the price fields through the coercion helper. The renderer names absent fields as 'not provided' so a reader can tell an omitted value from one the schema never asked for, and it keeps the trailing `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL: **BUY**` line for backward compatibility with code that searches for it.

sections.title: PortfolioDecision model and renderer
sections.explanation: The Portfolio Manager fills the final rating, executive summary, investment thesis and optional price target and time horizon in one structured call, with no separate extraction pass. `render_pm_decision` keeps the exact headers (`**Rating**`, `**Executive Summary**`, ...) that the memory log, CLI and report writers parse, which is why rating.py can read the rating line back.

sections.title: Sentiment report schema
sections.explanation: `SentimentBand` gives six discrete directions, and `SentimentReport` pairs a band with a 0-10 score (bounds enforced through `ge`/`le`), a confidence literal and a long narrative. The structured header replaces brittle regex parsing of prose. `render_sentiment_report` puts a deterministic band, score and confidence header in front of the narrative so the saved report can be read by people and parsed by code.

tradingagents/agents/state.py.overview: Defines the typed state that flows through the LangGraph workflow: `AgentState` for the whole run, plus `InvestDebateState` and `RiskDebateState` for the two debates. Every agent node reads from and writes partial updates to these channels. Tour step 5 introduces it as the data contract to learn before reading the graph itself.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: `MessagesState` from LangGraph supplies a `messages` channel with an append reducer, and `TypedDict` comes from `typing_extensions` for compatibility. `Annotated` attaches a human-readable description to each field without changing its runtime type.

sections.title: Investment debate state
sections.explanation: Tracks the bull/bear research debate: each side's history, the combined history, the latest response and a turn `count`. `ConditionalLogic.should_continue_debate` reads `count` and `current_response` to decide who speaks next or whether to hand off to the Research Manager.

sections.title: Risk debate state
sections.explanation: Tracks the three-way risk discussion between the aggressive, conservative and neutral analysts. Besides per-speaker histories and latest responses, it records `latest_speaker`, which the risk routing uses to rotate speakers in a fixed order.

sections.title: AgentState channels
sections.explanation: The top-level state extends `MessagesState` with the run's inputs (ticker, asset type, instrument context, trade date), the four analyst reports, the nested debate states, the investment plan, the trader's proposal and the final decision and rating. Later fields such as `past_context`, `memory_note` and `portfolio_context` are filled by the Memory Log step or supplied by the caller at run start. Reading this class top to bottom follows the order of the pipeline.

tradingagents/graph/propagation.py.overview: A small helper that builds the initial `AgentState` dictionary for a run and the keyword arguments for invoking or streaming the graph. TradingAgentsGraph calls it from `create_run_state` and `_run_graph`. Tour step 6 pairs it with the orchestrator as the piece that turns a ticker and date into graph input.

sections.title: Propagator setup
sections.explanation: The class keeps only the recursion limit, which the orchestrator passes in from `max_recur_limit` in the config. It imports the debate TypedDicts so the initial nested states are built with the declared shapes.

sections.title: Initial state construction
sections.explanation: `create_initial_state` seeds the message history with a single human message holding the ticker, stores the run inputs and contexts, and initializes both debate sub-states with empty histories and a zero count. Starting every report as an empty string means downstream nodes and the state logger can read any key without a KeyError, even when an analyst was not selected.

sections.title: Graph invocation arguments
sections.explanation: `get_graph_args` returns `stream_mode='values'` and a config dict holding the recursion limit and optional callbacks. The orchestrator later adds a checkpoint `thread_id` under `config['configurable']`, and `stream_run` overrides the stream mode to also receive task events.

tradingagents/graph/trading_graph.py.overview: The central orchestrator of the framework. `TradingAgentsGraph` creates the deep- and quick-tier LLM clients, compiles the LangGraph workflow, runs or streams a propagation inside a per-run config context with optional SQLite checkpointing, settles past decisions in the memory log, and records each run's state and decision. As tour step 6 notes, it imports more modules than any other file, and the CLI and `main.py` both drive the system through it.

sections.title: Imports and trade-date validation
sections.explanation: The imports bring together nearly every subsystem: config, data date windows, LLM client factory, memory, reflection, reporting and the graph helpers. `_validate_trade_date` accepts only a canonical `YYYY-MM-DD` string (round-tripping through `strptime`/`strftime` rejects forms like `2024-1-5`) and refuses future dates, so historical runs stay point-in-time.

sections.title: Checkpoint signature exclusions
sections.explanation: `_NOT_IN_SIGNATURE` lists config keys that do not change what a run produces, such as file locations, checkpoint toggling and retry counts. Every other key is hashed into the checkpoint signature, so changing a model or vendor forces a fresh run instead of resuming stale reports.

sections.title: Constructor wiring
sections.explanation: `__init__` binds the config globally, creates cache and results directories, and builds the deep and quick LLMs through `create_tier_client` from step 4. It checks that `max_tool_rounds` fits under the recursion limit (each tool round takes two graph steps, plus the first turn and the wrap-up) and fails fast instead of crashing mid-run. It then assembles ConditionalLogic, GraphSetup, Propagator and Reflector, and keeps the uncompiled `workflow` so it can be recompiled with a checkpointer later.

sections.title: Instrument context and run signature
sections.explanation: `resolve_instrument_context` looks up the real company identity once so agents do not invent one from the price chart. `_memory_as_of` limits lessons to those already resolved by the trade date in historical runs. `_run_signature` combines analyst selection, debate depths, asset type, portfolio fingerprint, layout markers and a SHA-256 digest of the remaining config into the string that keys checkpoint thread IDs.

sections.title: propagate entry point
sections.explanation: The main public API validates the date, enters `run_config` (a ContextVar-scoped copy of the config from step 3) and a checkpoint scope, then delegates to `_run_graph`. It returns `(final_state, signal)`, where the signal may be `REVIEW` and should be checked with `is_review` before it is treated as a trade.

sections.title: Checkpoint lifecycle
sections.explanation: `begin_checkpoint` opens a per-ticker SqliteSaver, recompiles the graph with it and checks whether a matching checkpoint exists, then returns the deterministic thread ID. `checkpoint_input` returns `None` when resuming, because passing the initial state again would duplicate messages through the append reducer (#1249). `end_checkpoint` closes the saver and restores the plain graph, `checkpoint_scope` wraps the pair in a context manager, and `clear_checkpoint_on_success` drops the thread once a run finishes.

sections.title: Run settings and report paths
sections.explanation: `run_settings` is an allowlist of reproducibility metadata (version, providers, models, analysts, depths, vendors); endpoints, keys and paths are left out because a backend URL can contain credentials. `save_reports` and `default_report_path` give programmatic callers the same report tree as the CLI. `create_run_state` validates the date and asks the Propagator for the initial state with the instrument and portfolio contexts.

sections.title: Memory Log step and settlement
sections.explanation: `_memory_step` is a graph node that runs in parallel with the analysts. It settles due past decisions without waiting for another process that holds the log, then loads point-in-time lessons for the Portfolio Manager. Each phase catches its own exceptions and records a `memory_note`, so a memory failure degrades the report instead of aborting the run. `record_decision` writes the state log and stores the final decision and its rating in the memory log.

sections.title: Graph execution and streaming
sections.explanation: `_run_graph` builds the state, injects the checkpoint thread ID and either invokes the graph or, in debug mode, streams it and pretty-prints each message once, deduplicated by message ID. `stream_run` streams in `values` and `tasks` modes with `subgraphs=True`, because each analyst runs in its own subgraph and reports its messages only through task results. Every `next()` call runs inside a copied ContextVar context so tool calls see this graph's config even if the process-wide config changed.

sections.title: Final state logging
sections.explanation: `_log_state` writes a curated JSON snapshot of the run: reports, both debate histories, plans, decision, rating and run settings. `safe_ticker_component` rejects tickers that would escape the results directory, and `ensure_ascii=False` keeps non-English reports readable for people.

tradingagents/graph/analyst_execution.py.overview: Maps the user's analyst selection keys ('market', 'social', 'news', 'fundamentals') to declarative node specs (graph node name, report key, tools) and validates the selection into an execution plan. GraphSetup uses the plan to create one subgraph per analyst. Tour step 7 describes it as the step that turns analyst choices into an ordered plan.

sections.title: Spec dataclasses
sections.explanation: `AnalystNodeSpec` and `AnalystExecutionPlan` are frozen dataclasses, so specs are immutable values that are safe to share. Each spec records the selection key, the human-readable node name used in the graph and the CLI, the state key the analyst's report is written to, and its tool tuple.

sections.title: Analyst registry
sections.explanation: `ANALYST_NODE_SPECS` is the single registry of available analysts. Tools come from each analyst module's own `TOOLS` tuple, so the prompt's tool list and the ToolNode cannot get out of sync. The 'social' key is kept for compatibility with saved configs but maps to the Sentiment Analyst, which has no tools because it fetches its sources before calling the model.

sections.title: Building the plan
sections.explanation: `build_analyst_execution_plan` keeps the user's order, raises on unknown keys and requires at least one analyst. Failing early here produces a clear error instead of an obscure graph-compilation failure.

tradingagents/graph/checkpointer.py.overview: Provides LangGraph checkpoint persistence so an interrupted analysis can resume. Each ticker gets its own SQLite database so concurrent tickers do not contend for locks, and thread IDs are deterministic hashes of ticker, date and run signature. Tour step 7 covers it alongside the graph wiring, and TradingAgentsGraph's checkpoint lifecycle calls into it.

sections.title: Imports and per-ticker DB path
sections.explanation: `_db_path` turns a ticker into `<data_dir>/checkpoints/<TICKER>.db`, passing it through `safe_ticker_component` to block path traversal. It creates the directory on demand, so callers never need to prepare it.

sections.title: Deterministic thread IDs
sections.explanation: `thread_id` hashes `TICKER:date[:signature]` with SHA-256 and keeps 16 hex characters. Because the hash is deterministic, rerunning the same ticker, date and settings finds the earlier checkpoint, while any change to the signature produces a different thread and a fresh start (#1089). Omitting the signature reproduces the legacy ID.

sections.title: Checkpointer context manager
sections.explanation: `get_checkpointer` opens a SQLite connection with `check_same_thread=False`, because LangGraph may use it from worker threads. It calls `setup()` to create the tables and always closes the connection in `finally`.

sections.title: Inspecting the latest checkpoint
sections.explanation: `checkpoint_step` returns the step number from the latest checkpoint's metadata, or `None` when no database or thread exists. The orchestrator uses this to decide whether to resume (invoke with `None`) or start fresh.

sections.title: Clearing checkpoints
sections.explanation: `clear_all_checkpoints` deletes each database together with its `-wal` and `-shm` sidecar files, because SQLite keeps committed data there and deleting only the `.db` would leave data on disk. `clear_checkpoint` deletes one thread's rows from the `writes` and `checkpoints` tables and ignores `OperationalError` in case the tables were never created.

tradingagents/graph/conditional_logic.py.overview: Contains the routing functions LangGraph calls after each debate turn to choose the next speaker or hand off. The investment debate alternates between bull and bear, and the risk debate rotates aggressive, conservative, neutral, both stopping at a configurable number of rounds. Tour step 7 describes it as the logic that decides when each debate continues.

sections.title: Round limits
sections.explanation: The class stores `max_debate_rounds` and `max_risk_discuss_rounds` from config. Keeping routing in a class with injected limits keeps the graph definition free of numeric constants and makes the routers easy to unit-test.

sections.title: Investment debate router
sections.explanation: The debate ends after `2 * max_debate_rounds` turns (one round means each side speaks once) and routes to the Research Manager. Otherwise the next speaker depends on whether the latest response starts with 'Bull'. This prefix convention is fragile, which is why setup.py maps every possible return value in its path map.

sections.title: Risk debate router
sections.explanation: The risk debate allows `3 * max_risk_discuss_rounds` turns before handing off to the Portfolio Manager, rotating Aggressive to Conservative to Neutral by checking `latest_speaker`. Any unexpected speaker falls through to the Aggressive Analyst, which keeps the rotation running instead of failing.

tradingagents/graph/setup.py.overview: Builds the LangGraph `StateGraph` for a run. Each selected analyst is wrapped in its own tool-loop subgraph, and those subgraphs run in parallel with a Memory Log node. The workflow then feeds into the bull/bear debate, the Research Manager, the Trader, the three-way risk debate and the Portfolio Manager. Tour step 7 centers on this file, and TradingAgentsGraph compiles the workflow it returns.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The file imports every agent factory from `tradingagents.agents`, LangGraph's `StateGraph`, `START`/`END` and prebuilt `ToolNode`, and the `WRAP_UP` message from the analysts' turn helper. It also uses the execution plan builder and ConditionalLogic from neighboring graph modules.

sections.title: Complete path maps
sections.explanation: `DEBATE_PATH_MAP` and `RISK_ANALYSIS_PATH_MAP` list every node a router can return. Every conditional edge driven by a router shares the full map, so a fall-through value caused by changed speaker labels can never hit a missing path_map entry and crash LangGraph mid-run (#1088).

sections.title: Analyst tool-loop subgraph
sections.explanation: `_analyst_graph` gives each analyst a private graph: the agent node routes to a `ToolNode` while its last message has tool calls, then back to the agent. Once `max_tool_rounds` is reached, `wrap_up` appends the `WRAP_UP` instruction and ends after that turn, so a model that keeps calling tools cannot reach the recursion limit (#1420). The subgraph's `output_schema` exposes only its report key, so parallel analysts never write the same channel and their tool chatter stays out of the shared messages.

sections.title: GraphSetup constructor
sections.explanation: GraphSetup holds both LLM tiers, the routing logic and the tool-round cap. Analysts, researchers, the trader and the risk debaters use the quick model; the Research Manager and Portfolio Manager use the deep model, as `setup_graph` shows.

sections.title: Creating agent nodes
sections.explanation: `setup_graph` validates the analyst selection, uses lazy factories so only selected analysts are instantiated, and creates every downstream agent with the appropriate LLM tier. Each analyst subgraph is added under its display name, followed by the fixed research, trading and risk nodes.

sections.title: Wiring edges
sections.explanation: All analysts and the optional Memory Log start from `START` in parallel, and the list form of `add_edge(first_steps, 'Bull Researcher')` makes the debate wait until every one has finished. The bull and bear nodes and the three risk nodes share conditional routers, while the Research Manager to Trader to Aggressive Analyst links and Portfolio Manager to END are fixed edges. The method returns the uncompiled workflow so the caller can compile it with or without a checkpointer.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/fundamenta.overview: Factory for the Fundamentals Analyst node, which studies a company's financial statements, profile and insider activity and writes `fundamentals_report`. It declares its `TOOLS` tuple, which analyst_execution.py reuses to build the analyst's ToolNode. Tour step 8 presents it as one of the analyst team's evidence gatherers.

sections.title: Imports and tool set
sections.explanation: The analyst gets five data tools: a fundamentals overview, balance sheet, cash flow, income statement and insider transactions. Declaring them as a module-level `TOOLS` tuple means the same object feeds the prompt's tool list, the model's tool binding and the subgraph's ToolNode.

sections.title: Role instructions
sections.explanation: The closure captures the LLM, and the node reads the trade date and instrument context from state. The system message asks for a detailed fundamental report ending in a markdown summary table, names when to use each tool, and appends `get_language_instruction()` so output follows the configured language.

sections.title: Prompt template
sections.explanation: The system prompt is shared boilerplate across analysts: it frames the agent as one collaborator among several, lists the tool names and states today's date, which the model must treat as 'now' for point-in-time tool calls. `prompt.partial` fills the template variables in advance, leaving only the `messages` placeholder for the conversation.

sections.title: Taking a turn
sections.explanation: `take_turn` (from turn.py) runs the model with the tools bound and returns the AI message plus the report text, which is non-empty only once the analyst stops calling tools. The node returns a partial state update; inside the analyst's subgraph the message is appended to its private history, and only the report key leaves the subgraph. Here the report is written to `fundamentals_report`.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/market_ana.overview: Factory for the Market Analyst node, which picks technical indicators, pulls price data and writes `market_report`. Its prompt contains a catalogue of supported indicator names and asks the model to treat a verified market snapshot as the source of truth for exact numbers. Tour step 8 introduces it as the price-and-trend member of the analyst team.

sections.title: Imports and tool set
sections.explanation: Three tools: `get_stock_data` for OHLCV CSV data, `get_indicators` for computed technical indicators, and `get_verified_market_snapshot` for authoritative figures. As in the other analysts, the `TOOLS` tuple is the single source for both the prompt and the ToolNode.

sections.title: Indicator catalogue prompt
sections.explanation: The long system message lists the allowed indicator identifiers (SMAs, EMA, MACD family, RSI, Bollinger bands, ATR, VWMA) with usage tips and asks for up to eight complementary picks. It requires exact indicator names because they are tool parameters, and asks the model to call `get_stock_data` before `get_indicators`. It also guards against hallucination: exact price or indicator claims must come from the verified snapshot, discrepancies must be flagged rather than reconciled, and validation claims need dated tool evidence.

sections.title: Prompt template
sections.explanation: The system prompt is shared boilerplate across analysts: it frames the agent as one collaborator among several, lists the tool names and states today's date, which the model must treat as 'now' for point-in-time tool calls. `prompt.partial` fills the template variables in advance, leaving only the `messages` placeholder for the conversation.

sections.title: Taking a turn
sections.explanation: `take_turn` (from turn.py) runs the model with the tools bound and returns the AI message plus the report text, which is non-empty only once the analyst stops calling tools. The node returns a partial state update; inside the analyst's subgraph the message is appended to its private history, and only the report key leaves the subgraph. Here the report is written to `market_report`.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/news_analy.overview: Factory for the News Analyst node, which combines company news, global macro news, FRED macro indicators and prediction-market probabilities into `news_report`. It adapts its wording to the asset type so crypto runs say 'asset' rather than 'company'. Tour step 8 presents it as the analyst that brings in world and macro context.

sections.title: Imports and tool set
sections.explanation: Four tools: ticker news, global news, macro indicators from FRED and prediction markets. The `TOOLS` tuple is shared with analyst_execution.py so the subgraph's ToolNode offers exactly what the prompt advertises.

sections.title: Asset-aware role instructions
sections.explanation: The node reads `asset_type` with a 'stock' default and picks the label 'company' or 'asset', which keeps the same analyst usable in the crypto pipeline. The f-string system message documents each tool's call signature with example indicator keys and topics, which helps the model form valid tool calls. It also asks for a closing markdown table and appends the language instruction.

sections.title: Prompt template
sections.explanation: The system prompt is shared boilerplate across analysts: it frames the agent as one collaborator among several, lists the tool names and states today's date, which the model must treat as 'now' for point-in-time tool calls. `prompt.partial` fills the template variables in advance, leaving only the `messages` placeholder for the conversation.

sections.title: Taking a turn
sections.explanation: `take_turn` (from turn.py) runs the model with the tools bound and returns the AI message plus the report text, which is non-empty only once the analyst stops calling tools. The node returns a partial state update; inside the analyst's subgraph the message is appended to its private history, and only the report key leaves the subgraph. Here the report is written to `news_report`.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/sentiment_.overview: Factory for the Sentiment Analyst node, the analyst from Step 8 that reads Yahoo news headlines, StockTwits messages and Reddit posts. Unlike the tool-calling analysts, it pre-fetches all three sources itself and pastes them into the prompt, so the model reports on data it was given instead of inventing posts. The output is a SentimentReport via structured output, with a free-text fallback for providers that do not support it.

sections.title: Module docstring
sections.explanation: Documents the three sources, the trimming to the analysis window, the optional Jev screening of social posts, and an honest caveat: these feeds only serve recent items, so a historical run's sentiment inputs are not point-in-time. It also explains why structured output is used: the band, score and confidence header reads the same across providers.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in the shared helpers: instrument context and language instruction, the Jev post screen, the SentimentReport schema and renderer, and the structured-output helpers. Note that `get_news` is imported from the tools module and called directly, and the Reddit and StockTwits fetchers are vendor functions rather than LangChain tools.

sections.title: Seven-day window helper
sections.explanation: Computes the start of a fixed seven-day lookback from the trade date. The sentiment window is not model-chosen; it is always the week ending on the trade date.

sections.title: Factory and structured binding
sections.explanation: `create_sentiment_analyst` binds the LLM to the SentimentReport schema once, at graph construction time, and returns the inner node closure. Binding outside the node avoids re-binding on every invocation.

sections.title: Pre-fetching the sources
sections.explanation: The node reads ticker and trade date from state, then fetches news via `get_news.func` (the raw function behind the tool, bypassing LangChain's tool wrapper), StockTwits and Reddit. The window is passed to the social fetchers so a backtest does not leak today's chatter (#1220). Each fetcher returns a string even on failure, so the model always sees either data or a clear placeholder.

sections.title: Prompt assembly without tools
sections.explanation: Builds the system message, then a ChatPromptTemplate whose wording deliberately avoids tool-range language: since data is already in the prompt, mentioning tools would invite a hallucinated tool call (#1130). The template is formatted into a concrete message list so the structured and free-text paths receive identical input.

sections.title: Invoke and return
sections.explanation: `invoke_structured_or_freetext` tries the structured model, renders the result to markdown, and falls back to the plain LLM if structured output fails. The node returns both a message for the conversation and the `sentiment_report` state field that the researchers read later.

sections.title: Subreddit character note
sections.explanation: `_build_system_message` first picks a one-line description of the subreddits being read: the default equity trio, a coin-specific community plus the broad crypto subs, or the broad crypto subs alone. This tells the model how to weight each community's tone.

sections.title: System message template
sections.explanation: A long f-string that wraps each source in explicit start/end markers and gives analysis rules: read the StockTwits bull/bear ratio with sample size in mind, look for cross-source divergences, separate events from opinion, and flag data limits in the confidence field. It ends by specifying each output field of the SentimentReport, keeping the score consistent with the band.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/turn.py.overview: A tiny but important helper shared by the tool-using analysts from Step 8. `take_turn` runs one analyst turn with tools bound, and, once the graph has injected the WRAP_UP message after the tool rounds are spent, runs a final turn with no tools so the analyst always finishes its report. `_as_text` rewrites tool-call history into plain messages for that final turn.

sections.title: Imports and WRAP_UP message
sections.explanation: WRAP_UP is the exact text the graph sends when an analyst has used its tool budget. Because `take_turn` matches on this content, the constant is the contract between the graph's routing and the analyst.

sections.title: take_turn
sections.explanation: If the last message is the WRAP_UP human message, the prompt's `tool_names` is overridden to say no tools remain and the model is invoked without `bind_tools`, because a model offered tools may still call one. Otherwise it invokes with tools bound. The second return value is the report, which stays empty while the model is still requesting tool calls.

sections.title: _as_text history rewrite
sections.explanation: Some providers refuse a history that contains tool calls when no tools are bound. This function converts each AIMessage with tool calls into plain text like `[Called get_news({...})]` and each ToolMessage into a HumanMessage holding the result, preserving the information while removing the tool-call structure.

tradingagents/agents/tools.py.overview: Defines the LangChain tools the analysts call (Step 9). Every dated tool receives the instrument and the run's `trade_date` from graph state through `InjectedState`, so the model never chooses the ticker and cannot fetch data past the trade date. Most tools clamp dates with `as_of` / `as_of_window` and then delegate to `route_to_vendor`.

sections.title: Module docstring and imports
sections.explanation: States the core rule: each dated tool takes the trade date from graph state and never serves data past it. Imports the date clamps from date_window, the error types, the router entry points and the verified snapshot builder.

sections.title: get_stock_data
sections.explanation: `symbol` and `trade_date` are annotated with `InjectedState`, so LangGraph fills them from state and hides them from the model's schema. The window is clamped with `as_of_window`; an unreadable window returns the error text to the model instead of raising, letting it retry with valid dates.

sections.title: get_indicators
sections.explanation: Clamps `curr_date` to the trade date, then splits the indicator argument on commas because models sometimes pass several at once. Each indicator is routed separately and a ValueError for one becomes inline text, so a single bad name does not fail the whole call.

sections.title: get_verified_market_snapshot
sections.explanation: Builds the deterministic snapshot directly rather than through the router. Its docstring tells the model to treat it as the source of truth for exact numbers. Vendor errors are converted to the router's sentinel strings because an exception escaping a tool would end the run.

sections.title: Fundamentals tools
sections.explanation: `get_fundamentals`, `get_balance_sheet`, `get_cashflow` and `get_income_statement` share one shape: an injected ticker, an optional frequency, and a `curr_date` clamped by `as_of` before routing. The `Literal` type restricts frequency to annual or quarterly in the generated schema.

sections.title: News tools
sections.explanation: `get_news` clamps a window like `get_stock_data`; `get_global_news` lets the model omit lookback and limit so config defaults apply; `get_insider_transactions` takes no model-supplied date at all and passes the trade date (or None outside a graph run) to the vendor.

sections.title: Macro and prediction-market tools
sections.explanation: `get_macro_indicators` documents the friendly FRED aliases directly in the argument annotation so the model sees them in the tool schema. `get_prediction_markets` passes the trade date through so the Polymarket vendor can decide how to handle a historical run.

tradingagents/dataflows/errors.py.overview: The vendor error taxonomy used by the router (Step 9). Every case where a vendor cannot return usable data derives from VendorError, and the subclasses correspond to distinct router reactions rather than distinct causes. New vendors raise these types and need no new except clauses in the router.

sections.title: Design docstring
sections.explanation: Explains the key principle: the number of exception types equals the number of distinct router reactions. Empty and stale data are handled identically, so they share NoMarketDataError and differ only in the `detail` text.

sections.title: VendorError base
sections.explanation: The common base class. Callers that only care whether a vendor failed can catch this one type.

sections.title: NoMarketDataError
sections.explanation: Carries the requested symbol, the canonical symbol actually queried (e.g. XAUUSD resolved to GC=F) and a free-text detail. The constructor builds a readable message from these, and the router later uses the fields to produce the NO_DATA_AVAILABLE sentinel instead of a vendor-specific empty string.

sections.title: VendorUnavailableError
sections.explanation: Signals throttling or a failed request. It says nothing about whether the instrument exists, which is why the router treats it differently from no-data and reports the vendor, not the symbol, as the problem.

sections.title: VendorNotConfiguredError
sections.explanation: Raised when a vendor's API key or config is missing. It inherits from both VendorError and ValueError, so older callers catching ValueError keep working while the router can treat it as a skippable vendor.

tradingagents/dataflows/router.py.overview: The data router from Step 9. It maps each tool method to its category and to concrete vendor implementations (yfinance, Alpha Vantage, SEC EDGAR, FRED, Polymarket), reads the configured vendor chain, and walks it with fallback. The typed errors from errors.py decide how each failure is handled and which sentinel string the agent finally sees.

sections.title: Vendor imports
sections.explanation: Imports every vendor implementation under a vendor-prefixed alias (e.g. `get_sec_edgar_balance_sheet`), so the mapping table below reads clearly. The config accessor reads the per-run ContextVar config from Step 3.

sections.title: TOOLS_CATEGORIES
sections.explanation: Groups tool methods into categories such as core_stock_apis or fundamental_data. Categories are the unit of vendor configuration in `data_vendors`, so one setting can switch all fundamentals tools at once.

sections.title: OPTIONAL_CATEGORIES
sections.explanation: Macro data and prediction markets are flavour, not core to a decision. When every vendor in these categories fails, the router returns a DATA_UNAVAILABLE sentinel instead of raising, while core categories still raise so a broken primary is loud.

sections.title: VENDOR_METHODS mapping
sections.explanation: The registry from method name to vendor name to function. Statement methods list SEC EDGAR between Alpha Vantage and yfinance; in the default (unconfigured) case the dict order becomes the fallback chain.

sections.title: Vendor lookup
sections.explanation: `get_category_for_method` finds a method's category, and `get_vendor` resolves the configured vendor: a tool-level entry in `tool_vendors` overrides the category-level `data_vendors` setting, with 'default' as the fallback sentinel.

sections.title: Sentinel messages
sections.explanation: `vendor_unavailable` and `no_data_available` produce the strings an agent receives when data cannot be served. Both explicitly instruct the model not to estimate or fabricate values, and the no-data message includes the typed error's detail (e.g. stale data) and the resolved symbol.

sections.title: Building the vendor chain
sections.explanation: Splits the configured vendor string on commas. An explicit configuration IS the chain: the router no longer silently falls back to vendors the user did not choose (#988/#289), which had produced cross-vendor inconsistencies. Only the 'default' sentinel uses every available vendor.

sections.title: Fallback loop
sections.explanation: Tries each vendor in order and classifies failures: unavailable, not configured, no data, or an untyped exception. Nothing is swallowed silently; untyped failures are logged so a broken primary stays visible (#989), and the first real error is kept for later.

sections.title: Final verdict
sections.explanation: Decides what to return after the loop. Any throttled or failed vendor means the chain cannot claim the symbol has no data, so it returns DATA_UNAVAILABLE. If every responding vendor said no data, it returns NO_DATA_AVAILABLE. Otherwise optional categories degrade to a sentinel and core categories re-raise the first error.

tradingagents/dataflows/date_window.py.overview: The shared point-in-time rules from Step 10, used by every dated data path to prevent look-ahead bias. It clamps model-requested dates to the trade date, trims dated items to a half-open window, reports windows a feed never observed as coverage gaps, and withholds live-only data (profiles, undated statements, insider trades) from historical runs.

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: Summarizes each rule in the module and the issues that motivated them. Note that dates are always handed to vendors as canonical YYYY-MM-DD strings because vendors compare dates as text.

sections.title: UTC normalization and in_window
sections.explanation: `to_utc` treats naive datetimes as UTC. `in_window` checks the half-open interval [start, end + 1 day). An undated item is kept only when the window reaches the present, because a backtest cannot prove an undated item is not from the future.

sections.title: Current date helpers
sections.explanation: `get_current_date` returns today as text, and `is_historical` compares a run date to it as a string, which works because both are canonical YYYY-MM-DD.

sections.title: coverage_gap
sections.explanation: Feeds like Yahoo news, Reddit and StockTwits return their latest items whatever window is requested. If the oldest returned item is newer than the window start, or the window extends past today, an empty result would falsely claim an absence, so this returns an explicit 'unavailable' placeholder instead.

sections.title: as_of and as_of_window
sections.explanation: `as_of` returns the model's date only if it parses and is not later than the trade date; otherwise it returns the trade date. It also canonicalizes '2026-7-3' style dates that would mis-compare as text. `as_of_window` clamps the end, shifts a window that lies wholly after the run date back so it keeps its length, and raises ValueError for unreadable or inverted starts (#1476).

sections.title: withhold_live_profile
sections.explanation: Company overview endpoints carry no historical vintage, so in a historical run this returns a notice explaining why profile fundamentals are withheld (#1300). Every fundamentals vendor applies this rule, so switching vendors cannot reintroduce the leak.

sections.title: Withholding undated trades and statements
sections.explanation: Two more notices with the same pattern: insider trades dated by trade date rather than filing date, and statements dated by period rather than filing date, are withheld from past runs because they may not yet have been public. The statement notice points to SEC EDGAR as the as-filed source.

tradingagents/dataflows/symbols.py.overview: Central symbol normalization for Yahoo Finance plus a path-safety validator for tickers. It maps broker, TradingView and MT5 style symbols (XAUUSD, EURUSD, BTCUSD, SPX500, HK and Shanghai codes) to Yahoo's conventions so a raw broker symbol does not yield an empty result the agents could hallucinate around. Supports the point-in-time vendors in Step 10, such as the OHLCV loader.

sections.title: Docstring mapping table
sections.explanation: A readable table of what users type, what Yahoo wants, and why. It also records the motivation (#781): centralizing the mapping means every yfinance entry point resolves symbols identically, and new instruments are added as table rows.

sections.title: Imports and logger
sections.explanation: Only logging and re are needed; the module is purely syntactic and makes no network calls.

sections.title: Lookup tables
sections.explanation: `_FOREX_CURRENCIES` and `_CRYPTO_BASES` drive rule-based detection, `_ALIASES` covers instruments that need an explicit mapping (metals and energy to front-month futures, index CFDs to Yahoo index symbols), and two regexes match HK and Shanghai codes.

sections.title: Crypto detection
sections.explanation: `_CRYPTO_QUOTES` is ordered longest first so USDT and USDC match before USD. `crypto_base` strips dashes and the broker '+' marker and returns the base only for known crypto bases; `_normalize_crypto` turns it into Yahoo's BASE-USD form, since Yahoo lists no stablecoin pairs (#982).

sections.title: normalize_symbol
sections.explanation: Applies the resolution order: aliases, crypto, six-letter forex pairs (=X suffix), zero-padded HK codes, Shanghai .SH to .SS, otherwise the upper-cased symbol. Non-string or blank input is returned unchanged, and any rewrite is logged at info level.

sections.title: safe_ticker_component
sections.explanation: Tickers come from CLI input or LLM tool calls, which prompt injection can influence. This validates length and an allowlist regex, and separately rejects all-dot values like '..' that the regex would otherwise allow, so a ticker can never traverse out of the cache, checkpoint or results directories.

tradingagents/dataflows/vendors/sec_edga.overview: The SEC EDGAR fundamentals vendor from Step 10. Because EDGAR reports every fact with its filing date, it can serve balance sheets, income statements and cash flows exactly as they were on file on or before the run date, restatements included at the vintage then current. It needs no API key, only an identifying User-Agent, and non-US tickers raise NoMarketDataError so the router falls through to the next vendor.

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: Explains why EDGAR is different from other vendors: they serve current values cut at period end, which is both pre-filing and post-restatement information. The Apple 2008 total assets example shows a restated figure that a point-in-time run must not see early.

sections.title: Endpoints and line-item tags
sections.explanation: Defines the ticker-map and company-facts URLs, a 24-hour cache TTL, and `_STATEMENTS`: for each line item, the XBRL tags filers use, best first. The first matching tag wins and values are never summed across tags, preventing double counting.

sections.title: Span and form rules
sections.explanation: `_SPANS` distinguishes quarterly (60-115 days) and annual (300-400 days) facts, since one filing reports both under the same end date. `_YEAR_TO_DATE` accepts 6- and 9-month cash flows labelled as such rather than subtracting filings, and `_ANNUAL_FORMS` restricts annual tables to 10-K, 20-F and 40-F reports.

sections.title: User-Agent, fetch and cache
sections.explanation: `_user_agent` uses SEC_EDGAR_USER_AGENT or a default with a placeholder contact address, because sec.gov returns 403 without one. `_fetch_json` turns every request or parse failure into VendorUnavailableError so the router can move on. `_cached_json` caches per day and writes atomically via `replace_file`; a truncated cache file is treated as a miss.

sections.title: CIK lookup and span index
sections.explanation: `cik_for` finds the zero-padded CIK in the ticker map, returning None for non-US filers. `_span_index` returns 0 for an instant fact (a balance) or the index of the span a duration fact covers, or None if it fits none.

sections.title: _as_of: values as known then
sections.explanation: The heart of the point-in-time logic. For each tag and unit, it skips facts filed after the run date, keeps the latest filing per (period end, span) so amendments count only from their filing day, and optionally requires annual forms. Earlier tags take precedence per period, and the filing's unit (USD vs USD/shares) is kept so EPS is not scaled like dollars.

sections.title: _statement table builder
sections.explanation: Resolves the CIK, loads us-gaap facts, picks spans for the frequency, and computes each line. Each row keeps its shortest reported span per period, and the output is one CSV row per period (#1517) with a header that states the as-of date and lists line items this filer never tagged.

sections.title: Formatting and public functions
sections.explanation: `_millions` prints USD in millions, with three significant digits for sub-million values so they are not shown as 0, and no thousands separators that would split CSV fields. The three public functions match the router's signatures; the income statement note explains that a fourth quarter is never derived by subtraction.

tradingagents/dataflows/vendors/yahoo/oh.overview: The Yahoo Finance OHLCV loader from Step 10. `load_ohlcv` resolves the symbol, serves a per-symbol five-year CSV cache when fresh, filters out rows after the as-of date to prevent look-ahead bias, handles unsettled trailing bars, and rejects stale frames. It feeds both the indicator tools and the verified snapshot.

sections.title: Imports and tuning constants
sections.explanation: `MAX_OHLCV_STALE_DAYS` (10) tolerates holiday weekends while catching the year-old frames yfinance sometimes returns (#1021). `OHLCV_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` (900) controls how soon a same-day cache is refetched so intraday runs pick up the close (#1150).

sections.title: Date and price cleaning helpers
sections.explanation: `_ensure_date_column` renames index/Datetime/date to Date. `_local_midnight` and `_normalize_dates` normalize each timestamp to its own naive local date, avoiding `utc=True`, which would shift non-US markets to the previous day (#1201). `_clean_dataframe` coerces prices to numeric, and `_fill_price_gaps` drops closeless rows and forward/back-fills gaps.

sections.title: Staleness guard
sections.explanation: `_coerce_ohlcv_dates` finds dates whether they live in a column or the index. `_assert_ohlcv_not_stale` raises NoMarketDataError with a stale-specific detail when the latest row is more than the allowed days before the requested date, so the router treats it as no data and tries the next vendor.

sections.title: Cache freshness
sections.explanation: A cache file only serves the day it was written. For a current-day request it is also refetched after the TTL, because Yahoo publishes a partial daily candle during market hours whose Close is not final and cannot be distinguished by inspecting rows.

sections.title: load_ohlcv setup and cache read
sections.explanation: Normalizes the symbol and validates it with `safe_ticker_component` before building the cache filename. It downloads five years up to tomorrow, since yfinance's end is exclusive (#986). An empty or Close-less cache is treated as a miss so a poisoned file is not served forever.

sections.title: Download with retry
sections.explanation: Uses `Ticker.history` instead of `yf.download` because the latter swallows rate-limit errors; `yf_retry` can then retry. Empty results raise through `raise_for_empty`, and only real data is written to the cache atomically.

sections.title: Point-in-time filtering and final checks
sections.explanation: Rows after the as-of date are removed. A closeless newest bar is an unsettled session, so it is dropped with a warning unless no bar has a close (#1289). Gap filling is optional: callers quoting exact prices pass `fill_gaps=False`. Finally the staleness guard runs.

tradingagents/dataflows/vendors/yahoo/sn.overview: Builds the deterministic verified market snapshot from Step 10, exposed to the Market Analyst as the `get_verified_market_snapshot` tool. Because an LLM can confabulate exact numbers (#830), this module computes the latest OHLCV row on or before the analysis date, a fixed indicator set and recent closes, and tells the model to treat them as the source of truth.

sections.title: Docstring, imports and indicator set
sections.explanation: Explains the motivation and fixes `DEFAULT_SNAPSHOT_INDICATORS` (EMAs, SMAs, RSI, Bollinger, MACD, ATR) so the snapshot has the same shape every run.

sections.title: _verified_rows
sections.explanation: Loads OHLCV with `fill_gaps=False`, because quoted exact prices must not include a filled cell carrying the previous session's price. It re-applies the as-of cutoff defensively, since a verification path should not trust its input to be pre-filtered.

sections.title: _fmt value formatter
sections.explanation: Formats values consistently: N/A for missing, dates as YYYY-MM-DD, and floats through the shared `price_text` helper.

sections.title: Computing indicators
sections.explanation: Wraps a copy of the frame with stockstats, which lowercases columns and adds indicator columns on access. Raw prices are read from the original frame. Each indicator is computed in its own try block so one failing indicator becomes 'N/A (ErrorType)' instead of sinking the snapshot. The recent-closes window is capped at 30 rows.
